Runs on this device's GPU in the background (WebGPU). It keeps going until you press stop; a stopped slice goes back to the pool. "stop after slice" finishes the current slice first, so its work counts.

ABOUT

Goldbach's conjecture says every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. It is unproven, and was checked up to 4×1018 by Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi. This network extends that check to 5×1018, in the open, with anyone's GPU. More about the conjecture: Dimostriamo Goldbach.

This project is inspired by their paper, Empirical verification of the even Goldbach conjecture and computation of prime gaps up to 4·1018 (Math. Comp. 83, 2014). Its figures, recomputed live from this verification: the live paper.

Each even n gets a pair n = p + q with p a small prime and q confirmed prime by a complete sieve; anything left over is settled by deterministic Miller-Rabin. Browsers run the same algorithm as the native B580 verifier (WebGPU + WebAssembly), and a browser slice only counts when a second device reproduces it bit for bit. Phones run a lighter mode (keep the screen on). The server itself verifies with its spare CPU. Raw board: /board (try: curl goldbach.net01.io/board).

## ABOUT

[Goldbach's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldbach%27s_conjecture) says every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. This project is inspired by their paper, [Empirical verification of the even Goldbach conjecture and computation of prime gaps up to 4·10^18](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-2013-02787-1) (Math. Comp. 83, 2014). Its figures, recomputed live from this verification: [the live paper](https://goldbach.net01.io/paper).

Each even n gets a pair n = p + q with p a small prime and q confirmed prime by a complete sieve; anything left over is settled by deterministic Miller-Rabin. Browsers run the same algorithm as the native B580 verifier (WebGPU + WebAssembly), and a browser slice only counts when a second device reproduces it bit for bit. # Goldbach conjecture verification, live paper: the statistics of 4×10^18 to 5×10^18

This page is inspired by, and follows section by section, [T. Oliveira e Silva, S. Herzog and S. Pardi, *Empirical verification of the even Goldbach conjecture and computation of prime gaps up to 4·10^18*, Math. Comp. 83 (2014), 2033–2060](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-2013-02787-1). Their verification stopped at 4×10^18; this project continues it. Each figure below is recomputed in your browser from the verifier's statistics as they arrive, next to [their published data](https://sweet.ua.pt/tos/goldbach.html) up to 4×10^18. Numbers refresh every 5 minutes.

Notation as in the paper. p(n) is the smallest prime p such that n − p is prime (the minimal Goldbach partition). S(p) is the least even n with p(n) = p. L(p, x) is the number of even n ≤ x with p(n) = p. ■ gold marks this project's data above 4×10^18; grey marks the paper's data.

## 1. Methods

Figures 1–2, live: time the native B580 GPU verifier needs per 10^12 integers, for each verified slice, against the slice's position x. The paper plots the time to sieve 2^30 integers on two 2012 CPUs; here the whole job (sieve and minimal Goldbach partition of every even) is shown.

## 2.1 Minimal Goldbach partitions

### Table 4, live: record-breaking p(n) above 4×10^18

Each row is an even n ≥ 4×10^18 whose p(n) is larger than that of every even between 4×10^18 and n (tracked for p(n) ≥ 3000). The record up to 4×10^18 is p(n) = 9781 at n = 3 325 581 707 333 960 528.

### Table 5, live: first occurrences S(p) found above 4×10^18

The paper's table lists 105 primes p ≤ 9769 that are never p(n) for n ≤ 4×10^18, so their S(p) is above 4×10^18. Because this verification runs contiguously upward from 4×10^18, the first even it finds with p(n) = p is S(p) itself: new mathematical data.

Figure 3, live: Q_1(p) = p / (log^2 S(p) · log log S(p)) for every known S(p). Granville's conjecture p(n) = O(log^2 n log log n) predicts that it stays bounded; the two refined constants 1.515 and 1.701 are dashed.

Figure 4, live: Q_2(p, x) = (L̂ − L) / √(2 L log log L) for every p < 250, where L counts the evens in [4×10^18, x] with p(n) = p in the exactly sampled segments (about 1 in 256) and L̂ is the Hardy–Littlewood prime k-tuple prediction for the same evens, from the paper's constants C_p,k. Values within about ±1 mean the conjecture predicts these counts as well as it did below 4×10^18. A new column is added every 5×10^15; the rightmost column is now.

Figure 5, live: Q_3(p) = e^π(p)/(0.755 log x − 4.19) L(p, x) / π(x) (top) and Q_4(p)Q_3(p) (bottom) for 2 ≤ π(p) ≤ 1000, at the current x. L(p, x) is the paper's count up to 4×10^18 plus this project's count above it (exact for p ≥ 3000, scaled from the sampled segments below). Circles: p mod 3 = 1; disks: the rest. Q_4 = 1 ∓ 0.04 Δ(p), Δ(p) = π(p; 3, 2) − π(p; 3, 1).

Figure 6, live: Q_5(p) = π(p) / (0.755 log^2 S − 0.755 log S log log S − 4.19 log S), S = S(p), for p > 1000. The paper's model of the decay of L(p, x) predicts Q_5(p) ≈ 1.

## 2.2 Prime gaps

g_k = p_k+1 − p_k is the gap after the prime p_k; P(g) is the smallest prime followed by a gap of exactly g; N(g, x) counts the gaps g with p_k+1 ≤ x. The verifier records every gap exactly in count and total length, and every gap ≥ 700 with its first occurrence (a bit-parallel test on every segment); the full N(g) and the sums of g^k come from walking every gap of the sampled segments (1 in 256), from the release that added the counter onward.

### Table 8, live: record gaps above the start of the gap data

### Table 9, live: first occurrences P(g) found above 4×10^18

The paper's table lists the gaps g ≤ 1474 never seen up to 4×10^18. The first time this verification sees one, above 4×10^18, gives P(g), as long as the gap data covers everything from 4×10^18 up to there.

Figure 7, live: Q_6(g) = g / log^2 P(g) for g > 4. Cramér's, Granville's (2e^−γ ≈ 1.123) and Shanks' conjectures are about its limit.

Figure 8, live: Q_7(g, x) = (N̂ − N) / √(2 N log log N) for 2 ≤ g ≤ 212, where N counts the gaps g in the sampled segments and N̂ is the Hardy–Littlewood prediction for the same integers, from the paper's constants A_g,k.

Figure 9, live: Q_8(g) = e^g/(0.960 log x − 3.58) (log^2x / x) N(g, x) / A_g,2, scaled as the paper's 5·10^−16 e^0.0266 g at 4×10^18, for 2 ≤ g ≤ 1000. N(g, x) is the paper's count to 4×10^18 plus this project's (exact for g ≥ 700, scaled from the sampled segments below), at x = 4×10^18 plus the span with gap data.

Figure 10, live: Q_9(g) = g / ((0.960 log P − 3.58)(log P − 2 log log P + log 2)), P = P(g), for g ≥ 100. The model of N(g, x) predicts Q_9 ≈ 1, close to Shanks' g ~ log^2 P(g).

### Table 12, live: prime gap moments

D_k = Σ g^k over the gaps in the range (D_1 exact; D_2…D_4 from the sampled segments, scaled to every gap), against the paper's fit D̂_k(x) = k! x log^k−1x Σ d_kn / log^nx (Heath-Brown's conjecture generalised).

### Table 11, live: twin primes and primes above 4×10^18

Exact counts from 4×10^18 to x against their predictions: primes against li(x) − li(4×10^18) and twin primes against 2C_2∫dt/log^2t, as parts per million.

---

Data: the B580 native verifier's exact statistics (every slice; sampled histogram on every 256th segment), synced every 10 minutes. Reference data: Oliveira e Silva's tables t0 and t1 (2012). Raw feed: [/api/results](https://goldbach.net01.io/api/results). Inspired by the work of Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi; any error here is ours.
